solution:
Expand along the first row:
\(2\begin{vmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{vmatrix} - (-5)\begin{vmatrix} 5 & 1 \\ 9 & 2 \end{vmatrix} + 7\begin{vmatrix} 5 & 2 \\ 9 & 0 \end{vmatrix}\)
\(= 2(4 - 0) + 5(10 - 9) + 7(0 - 18)\)
\(= 8 + 5 - 126 = -113\)
The value of the determinant is \(-113\).

Expand along the first row:
\(1\begin{vmatrix} 2 & -4 \\ 7 & 2 \end{vmatrix} - (-3)\begin{vmatrix} 0 & -4 \\ 9 & 2 \end{vmatrix} + 12\begin{vmatrix} 0 & 2 \\ 9 & 7 \end{vmatrix}\)
\(= 1(4 + 28) + 3(0 + 36) + 12(0 - 18)\)
\(= 32 + 108 - 216 = -76\)
The value of the determinant is \(-76\).

The second column entries are \(a_{12} = -1\), \(a_{22} = 2\), \(a_{32} = 1\). Their cofactors are
\(A_{12} = -\begin{vmatrix} 3 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 \end{vmatrix} = -(-6 - 0) = 6\),
\(A_{22} = +\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & -2 \end{vmatrix} = -2 - 0 = -2\),
\(A_{32} = -\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & -2 \end{vmatrix} = -(-2 - 6) = 8\).
Expanding along \(C_2\):
\(\Delta = (-1)(6) + (2)(-2) + (1)(8) = -6 - 4 + 8 = -2\)
The value of the determinant is \(-2\).

\(R_2 = (400,\ 600,\ 1000) = 200(2,\ 3,\ 5)\), so taking \(200\) common from \(R_2\):
\(\begin{vmatrix} 2 & 3 & 5 \\ 400 & 600 & 1000 \\ 48 & 47 & 18 \end{vmatrix} = 200\begin{vmatrix} 2 & 3 & 5 \\ 2 & 3 & 5 \\ 48 & 47 & 18 \end{vmatrix}\)
Now \(R_1\) and \(R_2\) are identical, and a determinant with two identical rows is zero.
The value of the determinant is \(0\).

Apply \(C_2 \to C_2 - C_1\) and \(C_3 \to C_3 - C_1\):
\(\begin{vmatrix} 101 & 102 & 103 \\ 106 & 107 & 108 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \end{vmatrix} = \begin{vmatrix} 101 & 1 & 2 \\ 106 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \end{vmatrix}\)
Now \(C_3 = 2C_2\), i.e. two columns are proportional, so the determinant is zero.
The value of the determinant is \(0\).

_note: Transcription flagged the (1,3) entry as printed '4x' with no exponent. Solved exactly as printed, and the book's own printed answer (2/3) is precisely what the printed form gives — so the un-squared entry is what the book intended and this is NOT a misprint. (With 4x^2 the rows would be the Vandermonde (1,2x,(2x)^2), (1,4,4^2), (1,1,1^2), giving x = 1/2 or 2, which does not match the printed key.)

solution:
Apply \(R_1 \to R_1 + R_2\):
\(\begin{vmatrix} x+y & y+z & z+x \\ z & x & y \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = \begin{vmatrix} x+y+z & x+y+z & x+y+z \\ z & x & y \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix}\)
Take \((x+y+z)\) common from \(R_1\):
\(= (x+y+z)\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ z & x & y \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix}\)
Now \(R_1\) and \(R_3\) are identical, so this determinant is \(0\).
Hence \(\begin{vmatrix} x+y & y+z & z+x \\ z & x & y \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = 0\).

Let \(\Delta\) be the given determinant (with \(a, b, c \ne 0\)). Multiply \(R_1, R_2, R_3\) by \(a, b, c\) respectively and divide \(\Delta\) by \(abc\) to compensate:
\(\Delta = \frac{1}{abc}\begin{vmatrix} ab+ac & abc & ab^{2}c^{2} \\ bc+ab & abc & a^{2}bc^{2} \\ ca+bc & abc & a^{2}b^{2}c \end{vmatrix}\)
Take \(abc\) common from \(C_2\) and \(abc\) common from \(C_3\):
\(\Delta = \frac{(abc)^{2}}{abc}\begin{vmatrix} ab+ac & 1 & bc \\ bc+ab & 1 & ca \\ ca+bc & 1 & ab \end{vmatrix} = abc\begin{vmatrix} ab+ac & 1 & bc \\ bc+ab & 1 & ca \\ ca+bc & 1 & ab \end{vmatrix}\)
Apply \(C_1 \to C_1 + C_3\); every entry of \(C_1\) becomes \(ab+bc+ca\), so \(C_1 = (ab+bc+ca)C_2\).
Two proportional columns make a determinant zero.
Hence \(\Delta = 0\).

Start from the right-hand side (with \(a, b, c \ne 0\)). Multiply \(C_1, C_2, C_3\) by \(a, b, c\) respectively and divide by \(abc\):
\(\begin{vmatrix} x & y & z \\ a & b & c \\ bc & ca & ab \end{vmatrix} = \frac{1}{abc}\begin{vmatrix} xa & yb & zc \\ a^{2} & b^{2} & c^{2} \\ abc & abc & abc \end{vmatrix}\)
Take \(abc\) common from \(R_3\):
\(= \frac{abc}{abc}\begin{vmatrix} xa & yb & zc \\ a^{2} & b^{2} & c^{2} \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = \begin{vmatrix} xa & yb & zc \\ a^{2} & b^{2} & c^{2} \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix}\)
which is the left-hand side.
Hence \(\begin{vmatrix} xa & yb & zc \\ a^{2} & b^{2} & c^{2} \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = \begin{vmatrix} x & y & z \\ a & b & c \\ bc & ca & ab \end{vmatrix}\).

The value of a determinant is unchanged when rows and columns are interchanged, so
\(\begin{vmatrix} l & m & n \\ e & d & f \\ u & v & w \end{vmatrix} = \begin{vmatrix} l & e & u \\ m & d & v \\ n & f & w \end{vmatrix}\)
In the right-hand determinant apply \(R_1 \leftrightarrow R_3\) and then \(R_2 \leftrightarrow R_3\):
\(\begin{vmatrix} l & e & u \\ m & d & v \\ n & f & w \end{vmatrix} \to \begin{vmatrix} n & f & w \\ m & d & v \\ l & e & u \end{vmatrix} \to \begin{vmatrix} n & f & w \\ l & e & u \\ m & d & v \end{vmatrix}\)
Each interchange changes only the sign, and there are two of them, so the value is unchanged.
Hence \(\begin{vmatrix} l & m & n \\ e & d & f \\ u & v & w \end{vmatrix} = \begin{vmatrix} n & f & w \\ l & e & u \\ m & d & v \end{vmatrix}\).

Let \(\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} 0 & a & b \\ -a & 0 & c \\ -b & -c & 0 \end{vmatrix}\). Interchanging rows and columns does not change a determinant, so
\(\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} 0 & -a & -b \\ a & 0 & -c \\ b & c & 0 \end{vmatrix}\)
Taking \(-1\) common from each of the three rows of this determinant gives
\(\Delta = (-1)^{3}\begin{vmatrix} 0 & a & b \\ -a & 0 & c \\ -b & -c & 0 \end{vmatrix} = -\Delta\)
So \(2\Delta = 0\).
Hence \(\Delta = 0\).

Expanding the given determinant along \(R_1\):
\(a(bc - 1) - 1(c - 1) + 1(1 - b) = 0\)
\(abc - a - c + 1 + 1 - b = 0\), i.e. \(abc - (a+b+c) + 2 = 0\) ... (i)
Now take the left side of what is to be proved (here \(a, b, c \ne 1\)):
\(\frac{1}{1-a} + \frac{1}{1-b} + \frac{1}{1-c} = \frac{(1-b)(1-c) + (1-a)(1-c) + (1-a)(1-b)}{(1-a)(1-b)(1-c)}\)
Numerator \(= 3 - 2(a+b+c) + (ab+bc+ca)\)
Denominator \(= 1 - (a+b+c) + (ab+bc+ca) - abc\)
Numerator \(-\) Denominator \(= 2 - (a+b+c) + abc = 0\) by (i), so numerator \(=\) denominator.
Hence \(\frac{1}{1-a} + \frac{1}{1-b} + \frac{1}{1-c} = 1\).

The three equations are consistent only if
\(\begin{vmatrix} k+1 & k-1 & k-1 \\ k-1 & k+1 & k-1 \\ k-1 & k-1 & k+1 \end{vmatrix} = 0\)
Apply \(C_1 \to C_1 + C_2 + C_3\); each entry of \(C_1\) becomes \((k+1) + 2(k-1) = 3k-1\), which comes out as a common factor:
\(= (3k-1)\begin{vmatrix} 1 & k-1 & k-1 \\ 1 & k+1 & k-1 \\ 1 & k-1 & k+1 \end{vmatrix}\)
Apply \(R_2 \to R_2 - R_1\) and \(R_3 \to R_3 - R_1\):
\(= (3k-1)\begin{vmatrix} 1 & k-1 & k-1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \end{vmatrix} = 4(3k-1)\)
So \(4(3k-1) = 0\).
\(k = \frac{1}{3}\)

Write the equations as \(3x + y - 2 = 0\), \(kx + 2y - 3 = 0\), \(2x - y - 3 = 0\). They are consistent only if
\(\begin{vmatrix} 3 & 1 & -2 \\ k & 2 & -3 \\ 2 & -1 & -3 \end{vmatrix} = 0\)
Expanding along \(R_1\):
\(3(-6-3) - 1(-3k+6) - 2(-k-4) = 0\)
\(-27 + 3k - 6 + 2k + 8 = 0\), i.e. \(5k - 25 = 0\)
\(k = 5\)

Let \(D = \begin{vmatrix} -1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{vmatrix}\). Expanding along \(R_3\):
\(D = 1\big[(-1)(4) - (2)(2)\big] = -4 - 4 = -8\)
Area \(= \frac{1}{2}|D| = \frac{1}{2}(8)\).
The area of \(\triangle ABC\) is \(4\) square units.

Let \(D = \begin{vmatrix} 3 & 6 & 1 \\ -1 & 3 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 \end{vmatrix}\). Expanding along \(R_1\):
\(D = 3(3+1) - 6(-1-2) + 1(1-6) = 12 + 18 - 5 = 25\)
Area \(= \frac{1}{2}|D| = \frac{25}{2}\).
The area of \(\triangle PQR\) is \(\frac{25}{2}\) square units.

Let \(D = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ -2 & 2 & 1 \\ 5 & 4 & 1 \end{vmatrix}\). Expanding along \(R_1\):
\(D = 1(2-4) - 1(-2-5) + 1(-8-10) = -2 + 7 - 18 = -13\)
Area \(= \frac{1}{2}|D| = \frac{13}{2}\).
The area of \(\triangle LMN\) is \(\frac{13}{2}\) square units.

Let \(D = \begin{vmatrix} k & 0 & 1 \\ 4 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \end{vmatrix}\). Expanding along \(C_2\) (only \(a_{32} = 2\) is non-zero):
\(D = 2 \times (-1)^{3+2}\begin{vmatrix} k & 1 \\ 4 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = -2(k-4) = 8 - 2k\)
Area \(= \frac{1}{2}|D| = 4\) gives \(|8-2k| = 8\), so \(8 - 2k = 8\) or \(8 - 2k = -8\).
\(k = 0\) or \(k = 8\)

Taken in cyclic order the vertices are \(A(0,-4)\), \(B(4,0)\), \(D(0,4)\), \(C(-4,0)\), and the diagonal \(AD\) divides the quadrilateral into \(\triangle ABD\) and \(\triangle ADC\).
For \(\triangle ABD\), expanding along \(C_1\) (only \(a_{21} = 4\) is non-zero):
\(\begin{vmatrix} 0 & -4 & 1 \\ 4 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 4 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = 4 \times (-1)^{2+1}\begin{vmatrix} -4 & 1 \\ 4 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = -4(-4-4) = 32\), so its area \(= \frac{1}{2}(32) = 16\) square units.
For \(\triangle ADC\), expanding along \(C_1\) (only \(a_{31} = -4\) is non-zero):
\(\begin{vmatrix} 0 & -4 & 1 \\ 0 & 4 & 1 \\ -4 & 0 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = (-4) \times (-1)^{3+1}\begin{vmatrix} -4 & 1 \\ 4 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = (-4)(-8) = 32\), so its area \(= \frac{1}{2}(32) = 16\) square units.
Area of the quadrilateral \(= 16 + 16 = 32\) square units.

Write the lines as \(x - y - 6 = 0\), \(4x - 3y - 20 = 0\), \(6x + 5y + 8 = 0\). They are concurrent if
\(\begin{vmatrix} 1 & -1 & -6 \\ 4 & -3 & -20 \\ 6 & 5 & 8 \end{vmatrix} = 0\)
Expanding along \(R_1\):
\(1(-24+100) + 1(32+120) - 6(20+18) = 76 + 152 - 228 = 0\)
So the three lines are concurrent.
Solving \(x - y = 6\) and \(4x - 3y = 20\): \(x = y + 6\), so \(4(y+6) - 3y = 20\), giving \(y = -4\) and \(x = 2\); this satisfies the third line too, since \(6(2) + 5(-4) + 8 = 0\).
The point of concurrence is \((2, -4)\).

\(\begin{vmatrix} 2 & 5 & 1 \\ 5 & 7 & 1 \\ 8 & 9 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = 2(7-9) - 5(5-8) + 1(45-56) = -4 + 15 - 11 = 0\)
Since the determinant is zero, the area of \(\triangle LMN\) is zero.
Hence \(L(2,5)\), \(M(5,7)\), \(N(8,9)\) are collinear.

\(\begin{vmatrix} 5 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 & 1 \\ 11 & 4 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = 5(-1-4) - 1(1-11) + 1(4+11) = -25 + 10 + 15 = 0\)
Since the determinant is zero, the area of \(\triangle PQR\) is zero.
Hence \(P(5,1)\), \(Q(1,-1)\), \(R(11,4)\) are collinear.
